segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Bell asks two shillings a night for the small room over the arch, and a further sixpence if a man wants a fire, and Captain Farr had taken the room and gone without the fire. He had eleven pounds and a half-pay warrant that would not be answered until the quarter. He had also a landlord who had known his great-uncle and was willing to chalk it up, which is a kind of charity that costs a man more than it saves him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On Saturday morning he crossed the green to the apothecary's, because he had been told to. Hester Lamb at Upper Barton, the next farm to Oakmere, had seen him go by her father's gate the evening before and cried out, and then been very cross with him for it. She had never believed him dead, she said, and she did not propose to start now. If he wanted the truth of that will, he was to go to Judith Vane, who was the one person in Amberlight who checked a story before she repeated it. Miss Vane opened the house door beside the shop with her sleeves pinned back and flour to the wrist.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: You are the second person in this parish to say anything to me that was true. Everyone else has said how glad they are.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: They are glad. They are only glad at a distance, in case it should cost them something.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She had known him since they were both children in the back pews at church, and she did not make anything more of it than that. She wiped her hands and took him through into the shop.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mr Owen Vane was at the counter scale with his sleeves rolled to the elbow and his apron white with chalk, and he heard his sister's nine sentences without stopping the scale. Then he said, flatly, that Mr Hartwell had an account with him. Camphor and a black draught since Michaelmas, paid at the quarter, which was more than half the parish managed. He supposed that was about to stop.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I am not asking you to quarrel with him. I am asking you what is in your book.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Owen said that when it was read out at Winchester with his name on it the quarrel would be his whatever she asked, and he had better know what it was a quarrel about. Then he went to the door and turned the card to Closed, in the middle of a Saturday morning, which Judith had seen him do twice in her life. The dispensing book came down, brown leather, ruled in four columns, and he ran his thumb along September.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The fourteenth, he said. Fenner, Oakmere. A draught against pain, and a strong one, carried out himself before nine because the boy had gone to Alresford. His hand, and his initial in the last column.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: The will is dated the fourteenth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then it was signed some hours after he had stood in the old man's bedchamber, said Owen. Fenner had known him at first, and called him by their father's name, and then could not get to the end of his own. Not his own name. He had tried it twice. Owen said it the way he would have read out a dose, and left the book open on the counter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The shop was quiet. Somebody outside dragged a barrow across the cobbles and the noise went off down toward the forge.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: It is not. It is a village apothecary's book against a gentleman's paper witnessed by two servants, and any attorney in Winchester will say a man may be heavy in the morning and clear by noon. It proves what he was given. It does not prove what he was when the pen was in his hand.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Somebody was in that room. Somebody held the paper for him and put her name under his.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Farr thought of an upstairs window and a hand pressed flat against the glass, and of a woman who had known him since he was seven years old standing there and letting him walk away.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Mrs Whitlow said nothing to you because she has been told what she is to say. I shall go up to Oakmere on Monday, and I shall take Mr Rowe, and we shall go about the parish alms, and nobody will think anything of it at all.
